title: Denary → floating point
intro: Catch up on the key A Level ideas. Complete four retrieval questions, work through the examples, then practise and explain your reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which type is suitable for a measured temperature of 12.75°C?
questions.feedback: A measured temperature may contain a fractional part.

questions.prompt: Convert 3C hexadecimal to eight-bit binary and denary.
Select −26 as an eight-bit two’s-complement integer.
Logically shift 10110000 left once in an unsigned byte. Which result and explanation are correct?
questions.feedback: 176 × 2 = 352 exceeds 255. Only eight bits remain, storing 96.

blocks.title: Read the format first
blocks.text: Throughout this lesson use an eight-bit two’s-complement mantissa and a four-bit two’s-complement exponent. The mantissa point is after its sign bit: weights −1, ½, ¼, ⅛, 1/16, 1/32, 1/64, 1/128. Exponent weights are −8, 4, 2, 1. Value = mantissa × 2ᴱ. There is no exponent bias.

blocks.title: Worked example: +6.5
blocks.text: 6.5 = 110.1₂ = 0.1101₂ × 2³. Pad the mantissa to eight bits: 01101000. The exponent +3 is 0011. Store 01101000 0011. Check: 0.8125 × 8 = 6.5.

blocks.title: Normalise without changing value
blocks.text: A non-zero normalised mantissa starts 01 if positive or 10 if negative. Shift left to remove redundant sign bits and decrease the exponent equally. For −0.5, 11000000 0000 becomes 10000000 1111: −1 × 2⁻¹. Zero is special; use all-zero fields. More mantissa bits improve precision; more exponent bits increase range.

questions.prompt: What is the denary value of binary 0.011?
Where is the binary point in the eight-bit mantissa?
questions.feedback: The leading bit has weight −1; the next has weight ½.

questions.prompt: Which leading pair identifies a negative normalised mantissa?
questions.feedback: 10 has no redundant leading sign bit.

blocks.title: Work through the method
blocks.text: Check the field widths before starting. Use the worked examples to guide each calculation, then read the feedback.

questions.prompt: Encode +10.5 using an eight-bit mantissa and four-bit exponent.

questions.feedback: Negate mantissa 01010100: invert 10101011 and add 1. Keep exponent +4.
Shift left twice and reduce exponent from 5 to 3.
Three left shifts give 01011000; decrease exponent 7 to 4.
11000000 0000 has the right value but is not normalised. −1 × 2⁻¹ is normalised.

writing.prompt: A pupil changes 00101000 0011 to 01010000 0011 and calls it normalisation (8-bit mantissa, 4-bit exponent). Explain the error and give the correct normalised pattern.
writing.model: The left shift doubles the mantissa, so leaving the exponent at 3 doubles the value from 2.5 to 5. Decrease the exponent to 2 to compensate. The correct pattern is 01010000 0010. Normalisation removes redundant sign bits and uses the available precision efficiently without changing the value.
checklist: I explained why the value doubled.
I explained that normalisation preserves value.

questions.prompt: Increasing the mantissa width can improve precision.
questions.feedback: More significant bits allow finer distinctions.

questions.prompt: Left-shifting a mantissa for normalisation requires an equal increase in exponent.
Zero must start 01 or 10 to be stored.
questions.feedback: Zero is a special case; all-zero fields represent it.
